title: The true approximation threshold for Sparsest Cut
short_statement: For nonuniform Sparsest Cut, the $O(\sqrt{\log n}\log\log n)$ algorithm and $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ SDP gap do not establish the computational threshold.
open_problem: Determine the nonuniform Sparsest Cut approximation threshold, improving the general-demand upper bound or proving matching computational hardness; distinguish the separate uniform-demand question.
background: Sparsest Cut is a clean mathematical abstraction of partitioning a network while preserving demand pairs. It is also the algorithmic face of a deep metric-embedding question: the flow-cut gap for a demand graph corresponds to how well certain metrics embed into $\ell_1$. Leighton-Rao type methods gave logarithmic approximations through multicommodity flow. The ARV theorem improved this to $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ for uniform demands using a geometric structure theorem for negative-type metrics from semidefinite programming. This was a conceptual breakthrough because it linked graph partitioning to high-dimensional geometry. The $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ lower bound is for nonuniform demands, not a matching uniform ARV gap. A better algorithm would need stronger convex relaxations, hierarchy rounds with new rounding, or a combinatorial method that avoids the known embedding obstruction.
full_statement: In the nonuniform Sparsest Cut problem, the input consists of an undirected graph or complete demand network on vertex set $V$, nonnegative capacities $c_{uv}$, and nonnegative demands $d_{uv}$. For a nontrivial cut $S\subset V$, define its sparsity by $$\Phi(S)=\frac{\sum_{u\in S,v\notin S} c_{uv}}{\sum_{u\in S,v\notin S} d_{uv}}.$$ The goal is to find a cut minimizing $\Phi(S)$. The uniform case has demands $d_{uv}=1$ for all pairs. Sparsest Cut is central to graph partitioning, multicommodity flow-cut gaps, and metric embeddings. The Arora-Rao-Vazirani framework gives an $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ approximation for uniform sparsest cut and balanced separator, and later work simplified and accelerated this guarantee. Naor and Young proved an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ integrality gap for the Goemans-Linial SDP relaxation, for nonuniform demands, so that relaxation cannot have smaller gap in that model. The general-demand upper bound is $O(\sqrt{\log n}\log\log n)$; the uniform-demand ARV bound must not be paired with the nonuniform lower bound as an exact match. The open problem is to determine whether polynomial-time algorithms can beat $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ by using stronger relaxations or non-SDP ideas, or whether a comparable hardness result holds under a standard assumption.
known_results: ARV gives $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ approximation for uniform Sparsest Cut and Balanced Separator. Arora, Lee, and Naor obtained related $O(\sqrt{\log k}\log\log k)$ guarantees for general-demand instances supported on $k$ demand vertices through embeddings of negative-type metrics. Sherman and Kolmogorov give faster and more parallelizable ways to realize essentially the same $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ approximation tradeoff. On the lower-bound side, Khot and Vishnoi refuted the constant-distortion Goemans-Linial conjecture and gave superconstant SDP gaps; Naor and Young later proved an $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ gap for the Goemans-Linial SDP. For general demands these upper and lower bounds leave a $\log\log n$ factor, and an SDP gap is not hardness against all algorithms. The nonuniform Naor-Young construction does not give the same uniform-demand gap.

progress.summary: Corrected uniform/nonuniform conflation. Nonuniform upper bound $O(\sqrt{\log n}\log\log n)$ and SDP lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ leave a gap; true computational threshold is not established here.

counterexample_rationale: Finite graph and demand instances can witness SDP or LP gaps and can falsify proposed rounding claims. They cannot by themselves prove complexity-theoretic hardness, but they are central evidence for barriers.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search over capacity-demand graphs and negative-type metrics can discover integrality-gap instances or stress-test stronger relaxations.

literature.synthesis: Keep demand models separate. ARV and its faster implementations give $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ for uniform demands. Arora-Lee-Naor give $O(\sqrt{\log n}\log\log n)$ for general demands, while Naor-Young give a nonuniform SDP gap $\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})$. Khot-Vishnoi provided foundational superconstant gaps. None of these relaxation lower bounds alone identifies the polynomial-time approximation threshold. New research-release claims concerning uniform gaps and constant-factor hardness were located but not theorem-reviewed in this audit; see the audit follow-ups.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Investigate stronger SDP or hierarchy relaxations; search for finite integrality gaps beyond Goemans-Linial; study whether small-set expansion or unique-games reductions can be sharpened into matching hardness; exploit special metric classes to identify structural decompositions that might generalize.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed $o(\sqrt{\log n})$ approximation must specify whether it handles uniform or nonuniform demands and must run in polynomial time. A claimed gap must identify the relaxation and prove both fractional and integral cut values. A hardness result should state its assumption and whether the factor is for uniform sparsest cut, nonuniform sparsest cut, or balanced separator. Do not confuse an SDP integrality gap with a computational lower bound.

where_posed.text: General computational threshold after the distinct uniform and nonuniform SDP results; see Naor-Young Section 1.7.3 for the model distinction.
